from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        self.wait(1)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Think of the sphere as thin horizontal rings.",
            "Project these rings onto the circumscribing cylinder.",
            "The cylinder's area equals the sphere's area.",
            "Everything sums up to four shadow areas.",
            "Calculus confirms the geometric proof."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Calculus Logic", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display a smooth curve with #FFFF00.
        curve = FunctionGraph(lambda x: 0.5 * np.sin(x*2) + 1, x_range=[-2, 2], color="#FFFF00")
        self.place_in_area(curve, "B1", "D6")
        self.play(Create(curve))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFF00")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw tiny vertical rectangles under the curve.
        rects = VGroup()
        for x in np.linspace(-1.8, 1.8, 10):
            h = 0.5 * np.sin(x*2) + 1
            rect = Rectangle(width=0.3, height=h, color="#00FFFF", fill_opacity=0.5)
            rect.move_to(np.array([x + 3.8, h/2 - 0.5, 0])) # Adjusted placement for the grid
            rects.add(rect)
        self.play(LaggedStart(*[Create(r) for r in rects], lag_ratio=0.1))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00FFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # "The cylinder's area equals the sphere's area." - simple color change
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # "Everything sums up to four shadow areas."
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#00FF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # "Calculus confirms the geometric proof."
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#FF8800")
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application", ["Sphere surface area is four times the shadow.", "Measure a planet's disk to find its area.", "This rule applies to any sphere."])
        
        # Create elements
        bridge = VGroup(
            Line(self.grid['C2'], self.grid['C5'], color="#00FF00"),
            Line(self.grid['C2'], self.grid['E2'], color="#00FF00"),
            Line(self.grid['C5'], self.grid['E5'], color="#00FF00"),
            Line(self.grid['E2'], self.grid['E5'], color="#00FF00")
        )
        load_arrow = Arrow(self.grid['B3'], self.grid['C3'], color=YELLOW)
        tension_label = Text("Tension", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        tension_label.next_to(load_arrow, UP)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(bridge))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FF00")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(Create(load_arrow))
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(Write(tension_label))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Geometric Bridge: Sphere Surface Area and Its Projected Shadow

sections.title: Prerequisite Visualization (1 min)
sections.content: Establish the relationship between a sphere and its orthogonal projection. Define a sphere of radius 'r' and a parallel light source projecting a shadow onto a plane. Explain that the shadow is always a circle with radius 'r', regardless of the sphere's orientation.
sections.example: Visualize a basketball held under a bright, high-noon sun; the shadow on the ground is a perfect circle, representing the 'cross-section' of the sphere.

sections.title: Connecting Area to Projection (1.5 min)
sections.content: Introduce Archimedes' Hat-Box Theorem. Explain that the surface area of a sphere is equal to the lateral surface area of a cylinder that circumscribes it. Mathematically show that the sphere's surface area is exactly 4 times the area of its projected circular shadow (4πr² vs πr²).
sections.example: An animation showing a sphere being wrapped by a cylinder; as we unroll the cylinder, we see it takes four 'shadow circles' to cover the sphere's entire surface.

sections.title: The Calculus Logic (1.5 min)
sections.content: Briefly demonstrate how the sphere's surface is composed of thin circular rings (frustums). As these rings are projected onto the circumscribing cylinder, they preserve their vertical height, revealing why the total surface area sums up to 4 × the shadow area.
sections.example: Animation of an orange being peeled into thin, horizontal strips, then flattened onto the cylinder's wall to perfectly fit the 4-shadow-area footprint.

sections.title: Real-World Application (1 min)
sections.content: Summarize the findings: The surface area of any sphere is 4 times the area of its largest projection. Apply this to light distribution or celestial bodies.
sections.example: Calculating the total surface area of a planet (like Mars) simply by measuring the area of the circular disk visible through a telescope (A = 4 × Shadow Area).
